list.listitem: Screen all adults 40 years and older for lipid disorders. A
Statins reduce overall mortality in primary and secondary prevention of CAD. A
Niacin, fibrates, and ezetimibe do not reduce all-cause mortality or cardiovascular (CV) mortality when added to statins. A

The 2022 USPSTF guidelines recommend a statin for patients between the ages of 40 and 75 years with at least 1 cardiovascular disease (CVD) risk factor and with a 10% or higher 10-year risk of CV events based on the pooled cohort equation.B

The 2018 ACC/AHA guidelines base treatment decisions on risk, emphasizing statins for patients with known heart disease, LDL ≥190 mg/dL, diabetics, and those with a 7.5% or higher 10-year risk of CV events. The British NICE guidelines recommend treatment with a 10-year event risk >10%. The 2020 U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs and Department of Defense guidelines recommend treatment at a 12% 10-year CV risk threshold.B

background.definition: Hyperlipidemia is a syndrome in which measured serum lipid components (total cholesterol [TC], LDL cholesterol, high-density lipoprotein [HDL] cholesterol, and triglycerides [TGs]) deviate from optimal levels.

list.listitem: Approximately 20% of all US adults have hyperlipidemia.
Hyperlipidemia is a major risk factor for CAD, which is the number one cause of death in the United States regardless of age or ethnicity.
Hyperlipidemia can exist as a purely primary disorder wherein abnormal levels result from inborn derangement of lipid metabolism and/or transport.
Secondary causes include diet, type 2 diabetes mellitus, cigarette smoking, obesity, hypothyroidism, chronic kidney disease, cholestatic liver disease, and drugs.
Problems with LDL receptor production or function lead to a lack of removal of LDL from the circulation, increasing serum levels, and, eventually, incorporation into atherosclerotic plaques.
In secondary hyperlipidemia, a combination of insulin resistance, increased intake of high caloric foods, or other endocrine abnormality results in altered lipid levels.
HDL ferries other cholesterols from the circulation to the liver, thereby reducing arterial deposition.
As LDL-laden plaques stanch off, blood supply and oxygen delivery to the body is compromised. The result of this in the myocardium is angina.
If the plaque grows excessively or ruptures, it can precipitate a clot, causing myocardial infarction.
The US Preventive Services Task Force (USPSTF) recommends screening adults between 40 and 75 years. B

Screening earlier may be considered in patients with risk factors such as type 2 diabetes, family history of early CAD, possibility of familial hyperlipidemia, or any combination of cardiac risk factors such as smoking, obesity, hypertension, or sedentary lifestyle. B
The USPSTF recommends screening adults between 40 and 75 years for lipid disorders.

Screening younger persons may be considered in the presence of risk factors such as type 2 diabetes, family history of premature CAD, possibility of familial hyperlipidemia, or presence of any cardiac risk factors such as smoking, obesity, hypertension, or sedentary lifestyle.

Patients do not have to be fasting. Non-fasting lipid panels provide similar or more accurate risk estimates than fasting levels. This is recommended by NICE, European Society of Cardiology, and other European guidelines.

Retesting is appropriate approximately every 5 years in average risk patients. Since guidelines have moved away from "treating to target," it is not clear whether there is any benefit to repeated testing in patients already taking a statin.

The 2018 ACC/AHA guidelines recommend that diabetics, anyone with LDL >190 mg/dL, and anyone with a 7.5% or higher risk of cardiovascular events be placed on a statin drug at a dose to lower their LDL cholesterol at least 30%.
The 2022 USPSTF guidelines recommend that patients between 40 and 75 with at least 1 CVD risk factor and with a 10% or higher 10-year CV event risk consider a statin (B recommendation).
The 2020 VA guidelines recommend treatment with a statin as primary prevention only for patients with a 12% or higher 10-year risk of a cardiovascular event.
As most trials only included adults 40 years or older, there are no clinical trial data to guide screening and primary prevention in younger adults.

The 2022 USPSTF guidelines both recommend that clinicians treat based on risk, and not use specific LDL targets. Higher risk patients receiving secondary prevention (those with known heart disease) should be placed on a high intensity statin if under 75 years old, and moderate intensity if over 75 years.
Niacin does not decrease mortality in patients with CAD or low HDL.
Follow the USPSTF recommendations for CAD risk stratification and corresponding lifestyle modification and/or statin treatment. A

A complete history can be useful to identify comorbidities and to assess CAD risk fully. Particular attention should be paid to modifiable risk factors such as tobacco use, sedentary lifestyle, alcohol use, diabetes, hypertension, and obesity.
Patients should be encouraged to modify these risks according to appropriate guidelines.
Lipid abnormalities rarely result in physical abnormalities, and most patients are asymptomatic.
A very high TC (>2000 mg/dL) may result in eruptive xanthomas or lipemia retinalis, and very high LDL may lead to the formation of tendinous xanthomas.
A nonfasting lipid panel can be the initial test. If the TC is greater than 200 or the HDL less than 40 for men, or less than 50 for women, then obtain an FLP for LDL determination.

Obtaining a thyroid-stimulating hormone level is a cost-effective way to determine whether thyroid dysfunction is contributing to lipid abnormalities. Other secondary causes of lipid abnormalities include nephrotic syndrome, anorexia nervosa, hepatitis, renal failure, Cushing's syndrome, and systemic lupus erythematosus.
reviews medications that can have deleterious effects on lipid levels.

The ACC/AHA Pooled Cohort Risk Equations are now recommended to assess 10-year cardiovascular risk, but greatly increase the number of adults eligible for statin treatment compared to ATPIII, especially adults age 60 years or older.Like other risk calculators, they somewhat overestimate cardiovascular risk.
Individualized screening guidelines are available from the USPSTF.
provides an approach to the diagnosis and treatment of hyperlipidemia.

Statins reduce overall mortality as primary and secondary prevention of CAD. A The US Preventive Services Task Force recommends statin therapy for adults aged 40 to 75 years with at least one CVD risk factor and a calculated CVD event risk of 10% or greater. B
Niacin with or without statins is not effective for the primary and secondary prevention of CVD. A
Ezetimibe with statins do not improve mortality or clinical fatal endpoints in patients with CVD. It is unclear if ezetimibe is effective as monotherapy or for primary prevention. A
Fibrates do not decrease and may increase overall mortality when used as primary prevention. A
Omega-3 fatty acids do not clearly demonstrate reductions in mortality. A
Herbal medications may improve cholesterol, but evidence that they improve patient-oriented outcomes is lacking. C

A systematic review identified 11 RCTs with 130,070 participants that compared targeting LDL < 70 mg/dl with targets >= 70 mg/dl. The median LDL levels achieved were 62 versus 103 mg/dl. At 2 years median follow-up, all cause mortality was lower (RR 0.94, 95% CI 0.89 - 1.00, NNT = 64) and a similar reduction in cardiovascular mortality (RR 0.90, ci 0.81 - 1.0, NNT = 67).

A study randomized 2860 patients with recent ischemic stroke or TIA to a target of LDL < 70 mg/dl versus a target of 90 to 100 mg/dl. After 3.5 years the compositive outcome of major adverse cardiac events (MACE) was slightly lower in the lower target group (8.5% vs 10.9%, p = 0.04, NNT = 42). The component seeing the greatest reduction was nonfatal stroke.

Statins and bile acid sequestrants target LDL, niacin targets HDL, fibrates and omega-3 fatty acids target TG, and intestinal brush border inhibitors may be added for further LDL reduction. Their effect on patient-oriented outcomes varies, though, with clear evidence of reduced cardiovascular events and mortality only for statins (see ).

Statins reduce overall mortality as primary and secondary prevention of CAD. For primary mortality prevention with statins, the NNT is 171 patients treated with statins for 5 years to prevent one additional death (). These studies included primarily patients without heart disease but with risk factors. Statins are more effective when used for secondary prevention: NNT = 50 patients with known cardiovascular disease treated to prevent one additional death. Statins are associated with a small increase in the risk of developing diabetes mellitus (NNH = 255).

In a large VA cohort of largely men with known atherosclerotic heart disease taking a statin, a propensity adjusted analysis found a graded "dose-response" association between increasing intensity of statin therapy and all-cause and cardiovascular mortality.

A secondary analysis of a large RCT with 20 years of follow-up found that statins for primary prevention reduced all-cause and cardiovascular mortality in persons with a LDL of 190 mg/dL or higher, regardless of risk level.
3 cohort studies suggest that more than 90% of patients who discontinue statin treatment due to adverse events can be rechallenged with the same or a different statin and be adherent 1 year later.
In patients older than 65 years without a history of cardiovascular disease and elevated LDL, statin treatment does not improve mortality.

A single large RCT (HOPE-3) enrolled adults with a mean LDL of 128 mg/dl (3.31 mmol/L) and randomized them to rosuvastatin 10 mg daily or placebo. There was only a very small reduction in the risk of a cardiovascular event (NNT = 91 over 5.6 years) and no mortality benefit.

A meta-analysis of 39 RCTs containing more than 117,000 patients conlcuded that therapies aimed at increasing HDL levels (eg, niacin, fibrates) did not reduce strokes, cardiovascular events, or mortality.
Niacin with or without statins is not effective for the primary and secondary prevention of CVD, based on a Cochrane review.
Fibrates do not decrease and may actually increase total mortality when used as primary prevention: NNT = −153.

A randomized trial with 10,497 patients with a median triglyceride level of 271 mg/dl, HDL 33 mg/dl and LDL 78 mg/dl randomized them to pemafibrate or placebo. While triglyceride levels were reduced, there was no difference in cardiovascular outcomes.
Ezetimibe (Zetia) reduces LDL cholesterol, but does not halt the progression of physiologic measurements of vascular disease.
PSCK9 inhibitors further reduce LDL cholesterol levels when added to statin therapy, but effects on patient-oriented outcomes are not known.
A phase 2 study of lepodisiran showed that it reduced lipoprotein(a) levels by 40% to 90% but clinical outcome studies are lacking.

Omega-3 fatty acids do not clearly reduce mortality when combined primary and secondary prevention data are analyzed. A 2005 meta-analysis reported a reduction in overall mortality (RR 0.77; 95% CI, 0.63-0.94). This review excluded an RCT of 3114 patients with angina. When this study was included in a subsequent review, reduction in mortality was not statistically significant (RR 0.98; 95% CI, 0.70-1.36). They may reduce mortality when used as secondary prevention: NNT = 28.
A polypill combining several agents (hydrochlorthiazide, atenolol, ramipril, simvastatin, and aspirin) lowers cholesterol to the same degree as simvastatin alone.
Garlic, red yeast rice, artichoke, and guggul may modestly reduce cholesterol, but patient-oriented evidence is lacking.
Guggulipid increases LDL and should not be recommended.
Vitamin E does not reduce mortality, recurrent events, or nonfatal stroke after an acute myocardial infarction.

Therapeutic lifestyle changes are generally recommended for all risk groups, whether medications are used or not. However, studies of the effect of dietary modification (for example low fat or low carbohydrate diets) has been limited to their effect on intermediate markers such as LDL cholesterol. A Cochrane review concluded that there is insufficient evidence regarding their effect on patient oriented outcomes such as cardiovascular events or mortality.
Moderate alcohol consumption (<30 g or 1 oz per day) increases HDL by 4 mg/dL and decreases CAD risk by 25%.
Smoking cessation increases HDL by 4 mg/dL and reduces total mortality in patients with CAD.
For each 30 mg/dL increase in LDL, the relative risk of CAD increases by 30%. C
The FLP can be repeated to monitor the expected effect of treatment, but statin dosing should be based on overall cardiovascular risk, and not titrated to meet arbitrary LDL goals. C

For each 30-mg/dL increase in LDL, the relative risk of CAD increases by 30%. This is based on observational data, though, so it does not necessarily follow that reducing LDL by 30 mg/dL reduces cardiovascular risk by the same amount.
The FLP can be repeated to monitor the expected effect of treatment, but statin dosing should be based on overall cardiovascular risk, and not titrated to meet arbitrary LDL goals.
Although statin package inserts recommend the use of liver function tests while the patient is on statin therapy, recent evidence suggests that routine monitoring may not be necessary.
A baseline CPK should be obtained before starting statin therapy and repeated only if patients experience symptoms of myopathies.
Statin therapy should be discontinued if the CPK is more than 10 times the ULN.
Patients with muscle soreness and no or moderate elevation in CPK (3-10 times the ULN) should be monitored weekly until symptoms improve or worsen to the point that statins should be discontinued.
The importance of medication compliance and smoking cessation should be addressed at each office visit.
As lipid levels have a low chance of increasing beyond age 65, there may be limited efficacy in continuing to rescreen this population if lipid levels are found to be in the normal range.
Statins prevent CAD but may have no effect on total mortality.
Statins are contraindicated in pregnancy.
Bile acid sequestrants, fibrates, niacin, and omega-3 fatty acids may be used when the potential benefit outweighs the possible risk.

It may be appropriate to screen children older than 15 years from families in which either primary hyperlipidemia is present or first-degree relatives have suffered an early myocardial infarction (<55 years in men and <65 years in women).
Guidelines for the screening and treatment of hyperlipidemia in children are available.
Diet is indicated as first-line treatment to achieve a TC of less than 215 mg/dL or an LDL of less than 155 mg/dL. Referral to a pediatric endocrinologist or dietician may be beneficial.
The use of drug therapy is determined based on the presence of family history of CAD. Bile acid sequestrants are considered first-line agents.
There is limited evidence to support existing treatment targets for hyperlipidemia in children.

algorithm.title: Lipid management for cardiovascular disease risk reduction (VA/DoD, 2025)

cell.label: Adult patient.

Comprehensive lifestyle medicine: a Mediterranean or other cardioprotective diet; 150 minutes a week of moderate or 75 minutes of vigorous physical activity; sleep 7 to 8 hours a night; social connections; stop tobacco and nicotine; minimize alcohol; manage stress; address overweight and obesity.
Is life expectancy limited?
Discuss the uncertain benefit of lipid-lowering therapy.
Existing ASCVD (MI or ACS, CABG or PCI, stable CAD, stroke or TIA due to atherosclerosis, or PAD; not asymptomatic atherosclerosis on imaging such as CCTA or CAC)?
Refer for cardiac rehabilitation if MI, ACS, or CABG/PCI in the past 6 weeks.

Very high-risk CVD (MI or ACS in the past 12 months on lipid-lowering therapy; recurrent ACS, MI, or atherosclerotic stroke on lipid-lowering therapy; or ASCVD and LDL-C 70 mg/dL or higher on lipid-lowering therapy)?
Diabetes, LDL-C 190 mg/dL or higher, or 10-year estimated risk 10% or higher?*
At least a moderate-dose statin. Consider referral to a lipid specialist if LDL-C is 190 mg/dL or higher.
HIV positive?
Moderate-dose statin.
Estimated risk 5% to <10% and the patient desires treatment?
No medication treatment.
Repeat the risk assessment every 5 years unless new risk factors develop.
Reassess therapy and consider modification if new risk factors or risk enhancers develop.
Three options: high-intensity statin; moderate-intensity statin plus ezetimibe; or moderate-intensity statin plus a PCSK9 inhibitor.
Start either a high-intensity or maximally tolerated statin plus ezetimibe, or a high-intensity or maximally tolerated statin plus a PCSK9 inhibitor.
Escalation needed?
High-intensity or maximally tolerated statin plus ezetimibe plus a PCSK9 inhibitor.
Monitoring: with a fixed-dose strategy, monitor lipids only for adherence or to verify the effect; with a treat-to-target strategy, monitor to an LDL-C goal of <70 mg/dL.
Re-emphasize lifestyle medicine: Mediterranean diet, exercise, smoking cessation, sleep, social connections, stress, and weight management.

footnotes.footnote: *Estimated risk from the PREVENT equations (American Heart Association).

Statin intensity: moderate is rosuvastatin 5-10 mg, atorvastatin 10-20 mg, simvastatin 20-40 mg, pravastatin 40-80 mg, lovastatin 40-80 mg, pitavastatin 1-4 mg, or fluvastatin XL 80 mg; high is rosuvastatin 20-40 mg or atorvastatin 40-80 mg.

Statin intolerance: a washout period (eg, 1 month), then the same or a different statin; a lower dose or nondaily dosing; or consider bempedoic acid, ezetimibe, fibrates, or a PCSK9 monoclonal antibody.
Persistent triglycerides of 150 mg/dL or higher on a maximally tolerated statin in secondary prevention: consider icosapent ethyl 2 g twice daily.

Source: VA/DoD Clinical Practice Guideline for the Management of Lipids for Cardiovascular Disease Risk Reduction, pocket card, December 2025 (US government work, public domain): healthquality.va.gov.
